# OpenCode V2 Permission System Behavior

How the V2 permission resolver actually behaves: the base policy every agent
inherits, why a catch-all rule inverts the default posture, how `external_directory`
interacts with `read`/`edit`, what the glob dialect can and cannot express, and
where permissions stop and policies begin.

> Provenance: [jewzaam/my-opencode-stuff](https://github.com/jewzaam/my-opencode-stuff)
> (source repo), [jewzaam/standards](https://github.com/jewzaam/standards/)
> (standards repo), [permissions](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions) and
> [policies](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/policies) (OpenCode docs).

## Default base policy

Every agent starts with the same ordered list, custom agents included
([docs](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions#defaults)):

```jsonc
[
  { "action": "*",       "resource": "*",            "effect": "allow" },
  { "action": "read",    "resource": "*.env",        "effect": "ask"   },
  { "action": "read",    "resource": "*.env.*",      "effect": "ask"   },
  { "action": "read",    "resource": "*.env.example","effect": "allow" }
]
```

Three consequences follow from this ordering:

1. The posture is permissive, not permissive-with-exceptions. Anything not
   mentioned anywhere resolves to `allow` because the first entry matches every
   action and resource.
2. Only reads of dotenv files are gated, and only by `ask`. `*.env.example`
   is carved back out to `allow` by the later rule.
3. No entry mentions `external_directory`, so reads, edits, and writes outside
   the active Location and its project worktree proceed without a prompt.
   The shipped Build agent therefore allows tools and out-of-workspace access
   with no configuration at all.

The docs also state "if no rule matches, OpenCode uses `ask`". That describes
the resolver in isolation. In a live session the base policy is always present,
so its leading `allow` is the rule that matches first — the practical default is
`allow`.

## The catch-all flip

Configuration is appended after the base policy, ordering rules
`lowest → highest` priority, and `last match wins`. A leading rule in user or
project config therefore sits after the base `allow` and overrides it:

```jsonc
[{ "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }]
```

Every action with no later matching rule becomes `ask`. This is the whole
mechanism behind "default deny-ish" configurations — the base policy is not
removed or reordered, it is simply out-voted by a later broad match.

Two symmetrical facts:

| Configured catch-all | Result for unmentioned actions |
|----------------------|-------------------------------|
| `* * ask` present    | `ask` — the catch-all is the last match |
| Catch-all omitted    | `allow` — the base `allow` is the last match |

A config that lists only narrow `deny` rules without a catch-all is therefore
still allow-everything-else, which is the common surprise. `deny` rules work
because they match after the base `allow`, not because the default changed.

Agent rules are appended after global rules and do not replace the global array.
Evaluation across several resources in one operation is `any deny` → deny,
otherwise `any ask` → ask, otherwise allow.

## `external_directory` is an independent check

`external_directory` is its own action, not a sub-case of `read` or `edit`. For a
path outside both the active Location and its non-root project worktree,
OpenCode checks the directory boundary against `external_directory` **before**
checking the path against `read` or `edit`
([docs](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions#directories)). The resource is a
canonical directory boundary, normally ending in `/*`.

The two checks are additive, not substitutive:

| Configured | Effect on external reads/edits |
|------------|-------------------------------|
| `external_directory * allow` only | Boundary check passes; `read` and `edit` still decide, so no automatic grant |
| `edit * allow` in the merged list | Every external edit allowed, because `*` matches `*`-spanning absolute paths too |
| `external_directory * ask` | Prompt on boundary before any `read`/`edit` rule runs |

The hazard is the combination. Approving a new external directory at runtime
("Allow always") writes a durable `allow` for that boundary, and if a blanket
`edit * allow` is already in the merged list, the newly approved directory is
immediately editable as well. Approving read access to a directory as a side
effect grants write access inside it.

`external_directory` covers external paths used by `read`, `edit`, `write`, and
`patch`. Shell additionally checks its external working directory and the
directories its scanner infers before checking `shell` resources.

## Glob semantics

Patterns are whole-value wildcards over normalized values
([docs](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions#matching)):

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `*` | Zero or more characters, including `/` and `.` |
| `?` | Exactly one character |
| anything else | Literal |

There is no regex mode, no alternation, no character classes, and no negation
operator. The pattern must match the entire normalized value, so a substring
pattern in the middle of a path matches nothing unless the surrounding text is
accounted for with `*`. `**` is not a distinct token — two adjacent `*` admit
exactly the same set of values as one.

Two boundary facts worth remembering:

1. A pattern ending in a space-and-star (`"git status *"`) additionally matches
   the same value with that trailing space-and-star removed, so it covers both
   `git status` and `git status --short`.
2. Because `*` spans `/`, a pattern beginning with `*` also matches absolute
   paths. No pattern can express "does not start with `/`" — the dialect has no
   negation, and `?` matches only one character without excluding `/`.

Shell resources are raw command text and are not home-expanded; shell matching
uses the same wildcard rules with `:`-prefixed resources in policies.

## Runtime path expansion

Only four forms are expanded: a leading `~`, `~/`, `$HOME`, or `$HOME/`. Expansion
happens once, when configuration loads, and applies to `read`, `edit`, and
`external_directory` resources.

| Written | Resolved |
|---------|----------|
| `~/projects/reference/*` | home-expanded at load time |
| `$HOME/reference/*` | home-expanded at load time |
| `$PWD/**` | literal text — matches nothing |
| `./tests/*` | literal text — matches nothing |

`{env:VAR}` substitution exists for config strings generally, but it resolves at
load time against the serving process's environment. It cannot express "the
current project", because the serving process is not the project. There is no
template that resolves per-session or per-call.

## Relative vs absolute resources

Path resources are not passed in one consistent form:

- In-project paths are passed Location-relative (e.g. `tests/unit/test_x.py`).
- Paths outside the Location are canonical absolute (e.g. `/etc/hosts`).

The permissions table states this only for `read`. Verified empirically for
`edit`: a rule `edit tests/**` matched an in-project edit and the write applied.
`edit` behaves the same as `read` here.

Since relative paths never begin with `/`, the pair

```jsonc
[
  { "action": "edit", "resource": "*",  "effect": "allow" },
  { "action": "edit", "resource": "/*", "effect": "ask"   }
]
```

scopes edits to the project while still catching every external directory —
including directories approved later, whose canonical absolute paths also start
with `/`. This is the ordering-safe alternative to relying on
`external_directory` alone.

Note the interaction with a broad `external_directory * allow`: the boundary
check passes silently, but the `edit /*` rule still fires on the absolute path,
so the prompt is preserved. Conversely, `edit * allow` with no `/*` tail is what
makes runtime external approvals grant writes.

## Plan is not a read-only boundary

The shipped Plan agent denies edits except files under the OpenCode plan
directory (`~/.opencode/plan`), and allows questions. Nothing in its policy
restricts shell:

| Agent | Shell behavior |
|-------|----------------|
| `build` | Permission-controlled by the merged rules |
| `plan` | Permission-controlled by the same merged rules — no extra restriction |
| `general` | Denies questions and launching subagents |
| `explore` | Denies everything except shell, reads, globs, grep, web fetches, web searches, and external directories |
| `title`, `summary` | Deny all actions |
| `compaction` | Base policy only |

Plan mode is a planning posture, not a sandbox. A shell command under Plan can
still modify files, delete them, or push, subject only to whatever `shell` rules
are configured. Any task that depends on Plan being read-only has to add the
`shell` deny itself.

Custom subagents follow the same principle from the other direction: they use
their own permissions, not a subset of the parent's. A parent that denies edits
does not constrain a child that allows them.

## Policies are separate from permissions

Policies are a second, independent layer
([docs](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/policies)). They are binary (`allow`/`deny`
only), never prompt, and only ever tighten — an `allow` statement never grants
access, it only lifts an earlier broader `deny`.

`tool.use` is the statement that touches permissions. It hard-denies a permission
check after the rules and saved approvals have run, so it overrides both an
`ask` and a durable "Allow always" approval. The resource is
`<action>:<value>`, matched against every resource the tool checks:

```jsonc
{ "action": "tool.use", "resource": "shell:git push *", "effect": "deny" }
```

A denied check fails with `Blocked by configuration policy` rather than prompting.
When no policy statement matches, the action is allowed — policy absence is never
a restriction.

Precedence is inverted relative to ordinary settings. Nearer configuration wins
for permissions and settings; for policies, broader configuration is evaluated
later and therefore wins:

| Rank | Source |
|------|--------|
| 1 (highest) | macOS managed preferences |
| 2 | System `opencode.json(c)` |
| 3 | Connected OpenCode Console workspace |
| 4 | Global `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json(c)` |
| 5 | Direct `opencode.json(c)`; outer directories beat inner |
| 6 (lowest) | `.opencode/opencode.json(c)`; outer directories beat inner |

Within one file, statements keep their written order. A repository `allow` cannot
lift a global `deny`, and an organization `allow` lifts a lower-authority `deny`.

## Saved approvals

An `ask` resolution can be answered three ways:

| Choice | Reply | Scope |
|--------|-------|-------|
| Allow once | `once` | The pending request only |
| Allow always | `always` | Saves the tool's proposed patterns as project-scoped `allow` rules |
| Reject | `reject` | Rejects the pending request and every other pending request in that session |

Saved approvals are durable project-scoped `allow` rules and never override a
configured `deny`. The tool chooses the proposed pattern: some propose `*`, shell
proposes command prefixes, skills and subagents propose their IDs. A broad saved
pattern therefore enters the merged list at high priority and interacts with
everything described above — including the `external_directory` plus blanket
`edit * allow` combination.
